title: Food safety: why food that looks and smells fine can still make you ill

summary.text: At a picnic, nine of twenty-two people fall ill the next day, and nobody can see, smell or taste anything wrong with the food. Your child learns how scientists work out which food did it, by writing down who ate what. They grow yeast in a fridge, in a warm bath and on the kitchen counter, and watch how temperature changes how fast tiny living beings multiply. They press a clean finger and a soapy finger onto a slice of potato, and find out what 20 seconds of soap really does. They also pull the water out of a cucumber with salt, learn to read a food packet, and meet the microbes that are friends in the gut and a danger in the dal.
summary.art: A picnic cloth with idli, a bowl of coconut chutney, a lemon rice dabba and cut papaya, and a child with a notebook ticking a table beside it.

intro.hook: Stir a spoon of yeast into sugary water in four glasses. Put one in the fridge, one on the counter, one in a bowl of warm water, and one after heating it first. Two hours later, one glass is foaming up to the brim and the other three have barely changed. All four had the same yeast, the same sugar and the same water. What made the difference?
intro.text: Yeast is a microbe, a living being too small to see. The glass in warm water gave her the best conditions, so she multiplied fastest. The bacteria that make people ill behave in the same way. In this unit you test how temperature changes how fast microbes grow. You find out why smell is not a safe test, why a healthy cook can still pass on an illness, and how a table of who ate what can point to the guilty food. You also learn why salt and sugar keep food safe and how soap lifts microbes off your skin.
intro.art: Four glasses in a row: one in a fridge, one on a counter, one in a bowl of warm water and one beside a pan, with the warm one overflowing with foam.

outcomes: I can name the three kinds of food hazard, which are microbes, chemicals and hard objects, and give an example of each from a kitchen.
I can explain why a food that looks and smells fine can still make people ill, and why smell is not a safe test.
I can show, from my own yeast test, how cold, warmth and heat change how fast microbes grow, and say what the danger zone is.
I can explain how soap and rubbing take microbes off hands, using what I saw on my own potato slices.
I can explain how salt, sugar and drying keep food safe, by pulling water out of microbes.
I can read a food packet and say what the dates, the ingredients, the vegetarian mark and the licence number are for.
I can use a table of who ate what and who fell ill to find the likely cause of an outbreak, and say how sure I am.

terms.meaning: Something in food that could harm a person who eats it.
terms.example: A stone in rice, a pesticide on a brinjal and bacteria in old dal are all hazards.
terms.art: A plate of rice with a small stone, a brinjal with spray drops and a pot of old dal, each with a small warning mark.

terms.meaning: A microbe that can make a person ill.
terms.example: Salmonella is a pathogen that can live in raw eggs and chicken.
terms.art: A magnified drawing of rod-shaped bacteria with a small label that says pathogen.

terms.meaning: A poison made by a living being. Some microbes make toxins in food, and some toxins survive cooking.
terms.example: A mould on groundnuts can make a toxin called aflatoxin.
terms.art: A handful of groundnuts with grey-green dust on some of them, and a small skull-and-bones mark.

terms.meaning: A person who has a disease microbe in their body, and can pass it on, without feeling ill themselves.
terms.example: A cook who is a typhoid carrier can make others ill while feeling perfectly well.
terms.art: A smiling cook stirring a pot while tiny microbes drift from her hands into the food.

terms.meaning: When several people who shared a food or a place fall ill with the same illness at about the same time.
terms.example: If eight guests at a wedding have a stomach upset the next day, that is an outbreak.
terms.art: A long table at a wedding feast with several guests holding their stomachs.

terms.meaning: The time between eating or catching something harmful and the first sign of illness.
terms.example: Some food poisoning begins a few hours after the meal, and some begins after a day or two.
terms.art: A clock between a plate of food and a person lying down, with an arrow showing the waiting time.

terms.meaning: The fraction of a group who fell ill, such as 8 out of every 14 people who ate a food.
terms.example: If 8 of 14 chutney eaters fell ill, the attack rate for chutney eaters is 8 out of 14.
terms.art: A group of 14 people with 8 shaded, labelled attack rate.

terms.meaning: The range of temperature, from about 5 to 60 degrees Celsius, in which bacteria multiply fastest.
terms.example: A pot of rice on a kitchen counter in a Chennai summer is in the danger zone.
terms.art: A thermometer with a red band from 5 to 60 degrees, a snowflake below it and a flame above it.

terms.meaning: When microbes move from one food, hand or tool to another food that is ready to eat.
terms.example: A knife used for raw fish and then for cucumber carries microbes across.
terms.art: A knife with raw fish on one side and cut cucumber on the other, with tiny dots moving between them.

terms.meaning: Water moving through a thin skin from the less salty or sweet side to the more salty or sweet side.
terms.example: Salt on a cucumber slice pulls water out of the slice.
terms.art: A thin skin with fresh water on one side and salty water on the other, with arrows showing water moving towards the salt.

terms.meaning: Something added to food, or done to food, to keep microbes from growing in it.
terms.example: Salt in pickle and sugar in jam are old preservatives.
terms.art: A jar of pickle with a spoon of salt and a jar of jam with a spoon of sugar beside it.

terms.meaning: A date after which the food may no longer be at its best in taste or texture, though it may still be safe if it has been kept well.
terms.example: A packet of dry biscuits that is a week past its best before date may just be less crisp.
terms.art: A biscuit packet with a printed date and a slightly soft biscuit beside it.

terms.meaning: A date after which a food that spoils easily should not be eaten, because it might make people ill.
terms.example: A packet of fresh paneer carries a use by date, and should be thrown away after it.
terms.art: A packet of paneer with a bold use by date and a red cross over the date next to it.

terms.meaning: Something cheap or harmful that is mixed into food, usually to make more money or to change its look.
terms.example: Flour added to milk to make it look thicker is an adulterant.
terms.art: A glass of milk with a spoon of white powder being stirred in.

terms.meaning: A food that causes a strong reaction in some people, such as swelling or a rash, even in small amounts.
terms.example: Groundnuts, milk, eggs and wheat are common allergens.
terms.art: A packet with a bold label that says contains groundnuts and wheat.

terms.meaning: A visible spot made of millions of microbes, grown from a single microbe or a small group on a surface.
terms.example: A white spot on a potato slice, after a few days, is a colony.
terms.art: A potato slice with small round white spots on it.

terms.meaning: The habits that keep microbes away from our bodies and our food, such as washing hands and keeping a kitchen clean.
terms.example: Washing hands with soap before cooking is good hygiene.
terms.art: A child washing hands at a tap with soap foam on her fingers.

terms.meaning: How much of something enters the body. Whether something harms us often depends on its dose.
terms.example: A few harmful bacteria may do nothing, and a million of them may make a person ill.
terms.art: A small pile of dots beside a large pile of dots, with a smiling and a sick face above them.

terms.meaning: The trillions of bacteria and other microbes that live in the gut of humans and other animals, most of them harmless or helpful.
terms.example: Gut bacteria help digest the fibre in dal and vegetables.
terms.art: A drawing of a gut with a crowd of tiny friendly bacteria.

terms.meaning: When the body loses more water than it takes in, for example from vomiting or loose motions.
terms.example: A child with loose motions needs small, frequent sips of ORS to avoid dehydration.
terms.art: A child sipping a glass of ORS, with a water level mark on her body that is low and rising.

explanations.concept: Three kinds of hazard: microbes, chemicals and hard objects
explanations.definition: A food hazard is anything in food that can harm the person who eats it. There are three kinds: biological hazards (microbes), chemical hazards (poisons) and physical hazards (hard or sharp objects).
explanations.description: Most people think of germs first, and microbes are the biggest cause of food illness in the world. These are biological hazards: bacteria, viruses, moulds and tiny worms. Chemical hazards are poisons. Some are put there by people, such as pesticide left on a brinjal, a cleaning liquid in a cold-drink bottle, or a cheap colour added to sweets. Others are made by nature. A mould on groundnuts can make aflatoxin, and a green, sprouting potato holds a poison called solanine. Physical hazards are things that can hurt the mouth or throat, such as a stone in rice, a piece of glass or a bone. Thinking in these three groups helps a cook ask the right question about each step: what could go wrong here, and what would stop it?
examples: Biological: bacteria growing in rice that was left out all night in summer.
Chemical: raw red kidney beans contain a natural poison that is removed by boiling them hard for at least ten minutes.
Physical: small stones in rice, which is why we pick and wash it before cooking.
explanations.art: Three plates side by side: one with rice and tiny bacteria, one with a green potato and a skull mark, and one with rice and a stone.

explanations.concept: Why smell is not a safe test
explanations.definition: Microbes that spoil food are not the same as the microbes that make people ill. Spoiling microbes often change the smell and taste, but many harmful microbes do not.
explanations.description: Spoiling microbes live on the food itself. They break it down, and that makes sour smells, gas and slime. We evolved to dislike those smells. But the bacteria that make people ill, called pathogens, are mostly adapted to living inside bodies, at around 37 degrees Celsius. They do not need to break down the food to grow, so they can multiply in a dish that looks and smells perfectly normal. Some also make toxins that have no smell or taste. This is why a dish can seem fine, and still make half the guests ill. A bad smell is a good reason to throw food away. A good smell is not a reason to think the food is safe. What matters is how the food was handled, how long it sat warm, and who touched it.
examples: A pot of cooked rice left on the counter overnight may smell normal in the morning and still carry bacteria and a toxin that cause vomiting.
Sour dal smells bad, because the spoiling microbes have been at work. That smell warns us.
Cut fruit left in the sun can look and taste fresh, and still carry harmful bacteria from a hand or a knife.
explanations.art: A smiling plate of food with a cloud of invisible microbes drawn over it, and a nose with a question mark beside it.

explanations.concept: Toxins and spores: why boiling does not always fix it
explanations.definition: A spore is a tough resting cell that some bacteria make, and it can survive boiling. A toxin is a poison that bacteria or moulds make, and some toxins are not destroyed by cooking.
explanations.description: Boiling kills most bacteria, but not everything. Bacillus cereus is a bacterium found in soil and on rice. Her spores survive cooking. If the cooked rice is then left warm, the spores wake up, grow and make a toxin that causes vomiting a few hours later. That toxin is not destroyed by reheating. Staphylococcus aureus lives on skin and in noses. If she gets into food from a cook's hand, she can make a toxin that also survives boiling. Aflatoxin, made by mould on groundnuts and maize, survives cooking as well. So the best protection is to stop the microbes from growing in the first place: keep hot food hot, cool leftovers quickly, and throw away food that has been sitting warm for hours. Reheating does not undo the damage.
examples: Rice that sat warm for six hours should be thrown away, even if it is reheated until it steams.
A cook with an uncovered cut on a finger can pass Staphylococcus into a salad.
Groundnuts with grey-green dust on them should be thrown away, because cooking will not remove the toxin.
explanations.art: A pot of rice with a tiny tough seed-like spore inside and a thermometer showing boiling, with the spore still sitting unharmed.

explanations.concept: The danger zone: how temperature changes the speed of growth
explanations.definition: The danger zone is the range of temperature from about 5 to 60 degrees Celsius. In this range bacteria multiply fastest, and food should not stay there for long.
explanations.description: Microbes are living beings, and they grow at the speed that suits them. Below about 5 degrees, as in a fridge, their growth slows down a great deal. At minus 18, in a freezer, it stops, but the microbes are not dead. They wake up when the food thaws. Above about 60 degrees, most bacteria cannot grow, and many die. In between, the warmer it is, the faster they multiply, and many harmful bacteria grow best close to the temperature of our own bodies, around 37 degrees. A kitchen in Chennai or Hyderabad in May can be 35 degrees, which is well inside the danger zone. This is why cooked food should be eaten within about two hours, or cooled quickly and put in the fridge. A big deep pot cools slowly, so food stays in the danger zone for a long time. A shallow, wide dish cools much faster.
examples: Idli batter rises quickly in the Madurai summer and slowly in a Delhi winter, because the microbes grow faster in warmth.
A tiffin of curd rice packed warm and carried for five hours in a hot bag stays in the danger zone the whole time.
A pressure cooker reaches about 120 degrees, so it kills many things that a pot of boiling water would not.
explanations.art: A thermometer from minus 20 to 120 degrees with the freezer, fridge, danger zone, hot holding and boiling marked in different colours.

explanations.concept: Carriers: healthy people who can still pass on an illness
explanations.definition: A carrier is a person who has disease microbes in their body and can pass them on to others, without feeling ill themselves.
explanations.description: We tend to think that only sick people spread illness. But some people carry bacteria in their gut, nose or skin without ever becoming ill. If they cook or serve food and do not wash their hands well, they can pass the microbes on. Typhoid fever is spread in this way. The bacteria, Salmonella Typhi, can live for years in a person's body without causing any signs. The same is true of Staphylococcus on the skin, which many healthy people carry. This is why washing hands matters for everyone who handles food, even when they feel perfectly well. It is also why anyone with vomiting or loose motions should not cook for others until they have been well for a day or two. It is not a question of blame. A carrier is not a bad person. She is a person who needs the same simple habits as everyone else, and a chance to learn about them.
examples: A caterer who feels perfectly well can pass typhoid bacteria through a feast if she does not wash her hands well after using the toilet.
Many healthy people carry Staphylococcus on their skin, which is why a cut on the hand should be covered while cooking.
A cook with loose motions should stay away from food preparation until she is well.
explanations.art: A cook with a smiling face and a hidden crowd of tiny bacteria inside her, with a speech bubble that says I feel fine.

explanations.concept: How soap works, and why 20 seconds
explanations.definition: Soap molecules have one end that likes water and one end that likes oil. They lift oily dirt and microbes off the skin so that water can rinse them away. Rubbing for about 20 seconds gives the soap time to work.
explanations.description: Skin has a thin film of oil, and microbes stick to it. Water alone slides over the oil and leaves much of it behind. A soap molecule has two ends. One end sticks into oil, and the other end sticks into water. When you rub soap on your hands, the oily ends grab onto the oil and the microbes, and the watery ends hold on to the rinse water, so the dirt is pulled off and carried away. The rubbing helps too, because it pulls the film and the microbes off the skin. For some microbes, the soap also breaks their outer coat of oil and kills them. Scientists recommend about 20 seconds of rubbing, including the backs of the hands, between the fingers, the thumbs and under the nails. Dry hands well afterwards, because wet hands pick up and pass on more microbes than dry hands.
examples: Rinsing greasy hands with water alone leaves the grease behind. Soap lifts it off.
People who wash their hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet have less diarrhoea in many studies.
Singing a short song twice, or counting to 20, is a way to scrub for long enough.
explanations.art: A magnified drawing of a soap molecule with a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail, lifting a speck of oil with microbes off a fingertip.

explanations.concept: How salt, sugar and drying keep food safe
explanations.definition: Microbes need water. Osmosis pulls water out of a microbe when the food around her is very salty or sweet, and drying removes the water altogether. So salted, sugary and dried foods keep for a long time.
explanations.description: A microbe is a tiny cell wrapped in a thin skin. Water can pass through the skin, but salt and sugar cannot easily. When the food outside is very salty or sweet, water leaves the cell and moves towards the stronger salt or sugar. The cell shrivels, like a cucumber slice sprinkled with salt, and cannot grow. This is how lemon pickle, mango jam and honey keep for months or years. Honey has so little free water that most microbes cannot grow in it at all. Drying works the same way. Vadams, dried fish and flour keep because they have almost no water. But there are limits. A few microbes, such as some moulds, can grow in quite salty or sweet foods. A pickle with a wet spoon in it can grow mould, because the water dilutes the salt on the top. And salt fish that gets damp in the monsoon can spoil.
examples: Jaggery, honey and jam keep for a long time because their sugar holds the water tightly.
Raisins and dried figs are fruit with the water taken out by the sun.
A pickle covered with a layer of oil, and always taken out with a dry spoon, stays safe for a year.
explanations.art: A thin-skinned cell in salty water with arrows showing water leaving the cell, next to a salted cucumber slice releasing drops of water.

explanations.definition: A packet of food in India must show the name of the food, the ingredients, a date, a vegetarian or non-vegetarian mark, nutrition information and the maker's licence number. Each of these tells a buyer something important.
explanations.description: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, or FSSAI, makes the rules for food sold in India, under a law passed in 2006. Look for the green dot in a square for vegetarian food, or a brown mark in a square for non-vegetarian food. Ingredients are listed from the most to the least by weight, so the first one named is the biggest part. If sugar is first on a biscuit packet, there is more sugar than anything else. The nutrition table shows what is in 100 grams. A 14-digit licence or registration number from FSSAI shows that the maker is registered to sell food. Dates matter too. Best before is about quality, and use by is about safety. Packets also list allergens, such as groundnuts, milk, wheat or soya, because a small amount can seriously harm someone who is allergic. Labels with words such as preservative, antioxidant or INS followed by a number tell you what has been added.
examples: A packet of chips that lists oil and salt before potato says there is more oil than potato by weight.
A packet of biscuits that says 'may contain groundnuts' warns families whose child is allergic.
Fresh paneer with a use by date should be eaten before that date, and thrown away if it is later.
explanations.art: A biscuit packet with arrows pointing to a green dot, the ingredient list, the date, the nutrition table and a licence number.

explanations.concept: Finding the cause of an outbreak: who ate what
explanations.definition: When many people fall ill after sharing food, scientists ask each person what they ate, and compare the fraction who fell ill among those who ate each food with the fraction among those who did not. The food with the biggest difference is the main suspect.
explanations.description: Imagine a picnic where 22 people ate the same lunch and 9 fell ill the next day. You cannot smell the problem. So you write a table. For each food you count how many ate it and how many of them fell ill, and how many did not eat it and how many of them fell ill. The food everybody ate cannot be the answer, since it cannot explain why some did not get ill. A food that half the ill people and half the well people ate tells you nothing. The clue is a food where most of the eaters fell ill and very few of the non-eaters did. That is called a high attack rate among those who ate it, and a low one among those who did not. The table points to a suspect, but does not prove it. Scientists then test leftover food in a laboratory, ask when people ate and when they fell ill, and look for a way that microbes could have got in. This kind of detective work is how outbreaks at weddings, schools and restaurants are tracked down.
examples: At the picnic, 8 of 14 chutney eaters fell ill, and only 1 of 8 who did not eat it. Chutney is the suspect.
The time between eating and falling ill, the incubation period, can point to the kind of microbe. A toxin can act within hours, while a bacterium may take a day or more.
If every guest ate the rice, rice cannot be told apart from the others by this method, and other clues are needed.
explanations.art: A table with four foods down one side and four columns across for ate and ill, ate and well, did not eat and ill, did not eat and well, with ticks filled in.

explanations.concept: Friend or foe? The same microbe in different places
explanations.definition: Whether a microbe harms us depends on where she is, how many there are, and which exact strain she is. The same kind of microbe can be harmless in one place and harmful in another.
explanations.description: Your gut is home to trillions of bacteria. Scientists estimate that the human body holds about as many bacterial cells as human cells. Most of them are harmless, and many help to digest food and keep harmful microbes out. One of them, Escherichia coli, or E. coli, lives in the guts of almost everyone, and nearly all strains do no harm. A few strains make toxins, and they can cause serious illness if they get into food or water. In a bowl of yoghurt, lactobacilli are friends. In a pot of old dal, other bacteria are enemies. And the same yeast that makes idli batter rise will fill a sugary drink with froth and spoil it. This is why sorting microbes into good germs and bad germs is too simple. A better question is: which microbe, in which place, in what numbers, meeting which person?
examples: Most E. coli live quietly in the gut. A few strains in a contaminated salad can cause bloody loose motions.
Curd bacteria make milk sour in a useful way. The same sourness in a pot of sambar is spoilage.
A small number of Staphylococcus on your skin does no harm. A large number in a cream cake, kept warm, makes a toxin.
explanations.art: A gut drawn as a garden with many small friendly bacteria, and one bacterium in a salad bowl with a red outline.

explanations.description: India has some of the most loved street food in the world, from pani puri in Delhi to bajji in Chennai and vada pav in Mumbai. Millions of people eat it every day, and many cooks have fed the same families for decades. Some street food is as safe as any kitchen. Some is not. The honest answer is that it depends on the vendor, the water, the ingredients and how the food is kept. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has a scheme to train vendors and to certify clean street food hubs. What matters most is how long the food sat, what water was used and how hands and utensils were washed.
examples: Food fried in front of you in hot oil and eaten at once has had little time in the danger zone.
Cut fruit, chutneys, salads and water, which are not cooked, and may be made with unclean water, are the usual risks.
A busy stall, where food is cooked and sold quickly, may be safer than a quiet one where food sits.
explanations.art: A busy street food stall with a vendor frying bajji in hot oil, a line of customers, and a bucket and a tap beside it.

perspectives.explanation: Many street vendors have no clean running water, and wash plates in a bucket again and again. Chutneys and cut fruit sit in the heat, and ice may be made from untreated water. These are real sources of illness, so vendors need training and clean water.

Most street food is cooked hot in front of the customer and eaten at once. It is often fresher than food that has been stored. Banning it would take away the work of millions of people. Training and clean water are the answer, not a ban.

Choose carefully. Eat food that is cooked hot in front of you, from a busy stall, with a clean-looking cloth and plates. Avoid cut fruit, salad and ice in the hottest months, and carry your own bottle of boiled or filtered water.

explanations.concept: Are food dates a law of nature? Best before and use by
explanations.description: Every packet in India shows a date. The dates are set by the maker, who tests how long the food is good if kept as the packet says. Best before is about quality, and use by is about safety. But how strictly should we follow them? Many people throw away food on the day of the date, though it may be perfectly good. Others eat food long after the date, and become ill. Scientists and food waste campaigners disagree about where the balance lies. The answer may depend on the food, on how it was kept, and on who is eating it.
examples: A packet of dry biscuits may be just a bit softer a month after its best before date, if kept closed in a dry place.
A packet of fresh cut paneer or minced meat, kept at room temperature past its use by date, may be unsafe even if it looks fine.
A tin that is bulging or dented should be thrown away whatever the date says.
explanations.art: Two packets on a shelf with dates, a dry biscuit packet with a thumbs-up and a fresh paneer packet with a clock beside it.

perspectives.explanation: Dates exist for a reason. Foods that spoil easily, and foods for babies, older people and people who are ill, should not be eaten after the use by date. A rule is easier to follow than a long argument.

A huge amount of good food is thrown away every year because people confuse best before with use by. Dry foods such as rice, flour, biscuits and tins are often fine long after the date, if they are stored well.

Learn what each date means. Trust the use by date on fresh foods that spoil fast. For dry foods, check how they look and how they have been stored. Always be more careful with food for babies, pregnant women and the old.

agreed.text: Most food illness is caused by microbes or by the toxins they make, and it is prevented by keeping hands and tools clean, separating raw and cooked foods, cooking thoroughly, keeping food at safe temperatures and using safe water.
agreed.evidence: The World Health Organization's Five Keys to Safer Food are based on studies of how food poisoning outbreaks happen all over the world.

agreed.text: Bacteria multiply fastest in warm, wet food that is rich in protein or starch. Cold slows them, and heat above about 60 degrees Celsius stops them.
agreed.evidence: In laboratories, scientists grow bacteria at many temperatures and count them, and find the same pattern again and again. You can see a version of it with yeast in the glasses test.

agreed.text: Washing hands with soap and water lowers the risk of diarrhoea and other illnesses spread through food.
agreed.evidence: Trials in many countries, combined in large reviews, report that handwashing with soap lowers diarrhoea by roughly a quarter to a third.

agreed.text: Some toxins made by bacteria and moulds survive boiling, so cooking cannot undo food that has already gone wrong.
agreed.evidence: Laboratory tests show that the toxins of Staphylococcus, the vomiting toxin of Bacillus cereus and aflatoxin stay in food after heating, and outbreaks have followed cooked food that was left warm.

agreed.text: A person can carry and spread disease microbes without feeling ill.
agreed.evidence: Tests of healthy people have found typhoid bacteria in their bodies, and tracing outbreaks has led back to them.

agreed.text: Salt, sugar and drying keep food safe because microbes cannot grow without free water.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measure the free water in foods, and find that salted, sugary and dried foods have much less. Honey, pickles and dried fish have been kept this way for thousands of years.

agreed.text: Smell and taste are not reliable tests of whether food is safe.
agreed.evidence: Investigations of outbreaks have found illness from foods that looked, smelled and tasted normal.

challenging.claim: If I cook it well, it is safe.
challenging.for: Cooking kills most bacteria, and food cooked until it is steaming hot is much safer than raw food.
challenging.against: Toxins and spores can survive cooking. Food that is cooked and then left warm for hours, or touched by dirty hands or a dirty knife afterwards, can still make people ill.

challenging.claim: Food cooked at home is always safer than food from a shop or a street stall.
challenging.who: A common belief in many families.
challenging.for: At home we know who cooked it and how clean the kitchen is.
challenging.against: Many outbreaks are traced to home kitchens and family feasts. Safety depends on the habits of whoever cooks, not on the place.

challenging.claim: Some people have strong stomachs and never get food poisoning.
challenging.for: People differ. Some are less likely to be ill, because of earlier exposure or a healthy gut.
challenging.against: Everyone can be made ill by enough of the wrong microbes or a strong toxin. Babies, old people, pregnant women and people with other illnesses are more at risk.

challenging.claim: Washing raw meat or fish before cooking makes it safe.
challenging.who: Many cooks in India and elsewhere.
challenging.for: Washing removes slime, blood, scales and grit, and many dishes are better for it.
challenging.against: Washing can splash microbes onto taps, the sink and nearby food. Cooking thoroughly is what kills the bacteria, so washing does not make the meat safe. Some food safety agencies advise against washing raw chicken for this reason.

challenging.claim: Natural foods are safe, and chemicals are dangerous.
challenging.for: Many people want food without added chemicals, and some added chemicals have caused harm.
challenging.against: Everything is made of chemicals, including water and salt. Some natural things are poisons, such as aflatoxin on groundnuts, solanine in green potatoes and the natural poison in raw kidney beans. What matters is the dose and the substance.

challenging.claim: Antibiotics should be given straight away for any food poisoning.
challenging.for: Antibiotics do kill bacteria, and they are needed for some serious infections.
challenging.against: Most food poisoning gets better by itself in a day or two, and the most important treatment is to drink fluids such as ORS. Antibiotics may not help, can make some infections worse, and using them too often breeds bacteria that resist them. A doctor decides.

big_questions.q: The same E. coli lives quietly in your gut, and can make you ill in a salad. Is she a friend or an enemy?
big_questions.hint: Think about what she is doing in each place, and what changes between the two.

big_questions.q: Honey is full of sugar and has very little water, and it can keep for years. Why can microbes not live in it, when they love sugary water?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens to the water inside a microbe when the outside is very sweet.

big_questions.q: A healthy cook can make others ill without ever being ill herself. Should she be stopped from cooking? Who decides, and how?
big_questions.hint: Think about her job, her family, the guests, and what could make the risk smaller.

big_questions.q: When a feast makes people ill, who is responsible: the cook, the caterer, the guests or the government?
big_questions.hint: Think about who knew what, who could have stopped it, and who would pay for a fix.

big_questions.q: The table says 8 of 14 chutney eaters fell ill, and 1 of 8 non-eaters. Does that prove the chutney did it? What else would you want to know?
big_questions.hint: Think about the one non-eater who fell ill, and what a laboratory could test.

big_questions.q: Some people eat raw fish and are fine, and others get ill. How does anyone decide what is safe to eat?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the fish came from, how it was kept, who prepared it, and how often they have done so.

big_questions.q: Safe food costs money: clean water, fridges, training. Who should pay so that everyone, including the poorest, can eat safely?
big_questions.hint: Think about families without a fridge, vendors without a tap, and what a government, a school or a neighbourhood could do.

big_questions.q: You cannot see the microbes in your food. How do you decide what to trust when you cannot see the danger?
big_questions.hint: Think about rules, records, tests and the people who know more than you.

big_questions.q: A pickle keeps for a year and a dal spoils in a day. What does that tell you about what microbes need?
big_questions.hint: Think about water, salt, acid and oil.

big_questions.q: If most microbes in our bodies are harmless or helpful, is cleaning everything the best idea?
big_questions.hint: Think about which cleaning matters most, and where in the kitchen the real danger is.

story.title: The Picnic Table
story.note: A made-up story. Sharanya, Dr. Fathima, Mrs. Gowda and the school are invented. Kukkarahalli Lake is a real lake in Mysuru. The science is real. Health officers do trace outbreaks by asking who ate what and comparing how many ate and fell ill. A moist food, such as ground coconut chutney, that is made the evening before and kept warm can let bacteria multiply to large numbers. The numbers in the story are made up, and they are chosen to show the method.
text: The Class 4 picnic was at Kukkarahalli Lake in Mysuru. There were twenty children and two teachers. They spread one big cloth under a tamarind tree, and Padma Miss laid out the food that families had sent.

There was lemon rice from Sharanya's amma. There were boiled eggs from the Fernandes family, and cut papaya from Chandan's house. There were packets of juice, and a big steel dabba of idlis from Mrs. Gowda, with a bowl of her coconut chutney.
Mrs. Gowda's chutney smelled of fresh coconut and curry leaves. It was the best smell on the cloth. Fourteen people had some. Sharanya did not. She did not like coconut.
Everyone ate and laughed. Nobody noticed anything wrong. The papaya was sweet, the eggs were soft, and the lake was bright in the sun.

The next morning, only thirteen children came to school. Padma Miss came in pale, and had to sit down. By lunchtime, nine people in all had been ill. Some had been sick in the night. Some had a bad stomach ache.

"It must have been the eggs," said one mother. "No, the juice," said another. The principal called the city health office, and a doctor came that afternoon. Her name was Dr. Fathima, and she carried a clipboard and a notebook.

"Can anyone smell what went wrong?" Dr. Fathima asked the class. The children sniffed. Chandan laughed. "No. We cannot smell a stomach ache." "Exactly," said Dr. Fathima. "So we ask questions instead. We find out who ate what."

She asked Sharanya to help, since Sharanya had not been ill and wrote very neatly. They drew a table on the blackboard. Foods went down the side. Across the top went four columns: ate and ill, ate and well, did not eat and ill, did not eat and well.
"Idli," said Dr. Fathima. "Who ate idli?" Every hand went up. "Then idli cannot be our clue," she said. "Everyone ate it. It cannot explain why some are ill and some are well."

Next was the lemon rice. Fifteen had eaten it, and six of them were ill. Seven had not eaten it, and three of those were ill. Sharanya looked at her numbers. "About the same either way," she said. "So not the rice." Dr. Fathima nodded.
The eggs, the papaya and the juice came out the same. Whether people ate them or not, about four in every ten were ill. Sharanya crossed them off one by one.

Then came the chutney. Fourteen had eaten it, and eight of them were ill. Eight had not, and only one of those was ill. Sharanya counted twice. The class went very quiet. "Chutney," said Chandan, in a small voice.
"But it smelled so good!" he said. "Yes," said Dr. Fathima. "That is why smell is a poor test. The bacteria that make people ill often do not change the smell or the taste."

A boy at the back put his hand up. "Miss, I did not eat the chutney, and I was ill." It was Raghu. "Good," said Dr. Fathima. "One that does not fit is a useful clue too. Were you unwell before the picnic?" Raghu nodded. "I had a stomach ache the evening before." "Then perhaps that was something else," she said. "A table points. It does not prove."

Dr. Fathima spoke quietly to Mrs. Gowda, who had come to the school, worried. Mrs. Gowda had ground the coconut with chilli and salt the evening before. She had left the chutney in a steel dabba on the counter all night. In the morning, she carried it to the picnic in a bag, in the back of a hot van, for three hours.

"Fresh coconut chutney is wet, and it is not sour, and it is not cooked after it is ground," said Dr. Fathima gently. "For bacteria, that is a feast. In a warm van, a few can become millions. You did what many kind cooks do. Nobody told you. Now you know." She took a spoon of the leftover chutney for the laboratory. Two days later, the lab report said it held a very large number of harmful bacteria.

The next picnic had a new rule. Chutney was ground that morning, kept in a bag with an ice pack, and eaten within two hours. Sharanya drew the table on a big sheet of paper, and Padma Miss pinned it to the classroom wall.

That evening, Sharanya wrote the table in her own notebook. At the bottom she wrote: a food that everyone ate cannot be the clue. Then she asked her amma if they could check the lemon rice dabba before the next trip.
story.epiphany: When food looks and smells fine, we can still find the cause by asking who ate what. The food where most eaters fell ill, and few non-eaters did, is the suspect.
ask: Why could Dr. Fathima not use idli as a clue, when everyone ate it?
Why is a table of who ate what more useful than smelling the food?
Raghu did not eat the chutney and was ill. Does that mean the table was wrong?
What could make a cook's chutney safer on a hot day?

how_we_found_out.story: In 1906, six people in a rented house at Oyster Bay, near New York, fell ill with typhoid fever, a serious illness spread by bacteria in food or water. The owner hired a sanitary engineer named George Soper to find out why. At that time, most people believed that typhoid spread only from people who looked sick, or from dirty water. Soper found that the family's cook, Mary Mallon, had left soon after the illness began. She had never been ill. He traced her to other homes where she had cooked, and found typhoid in several of them. In 1907, health officers, including Dr. Sara Josephine Baker, found her, and tests showed typhoid bacteria in her body. She was one of the first healthy typhoid carriers identified in the United States. She was kept apart on an island for years, and people still ask whether she was treated fairly.
how_we_found_out.who: George Soper, a sanitary engineer, and Dr. Sara Josephine Baker, with the New York health department
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people thought only people who looked sick could pass on typhoid. Tracing the illness from home to home, and testing a cook who felt perfectly well, showed that a healthy carrier can spread it.

roots.context: We have grown yeast, pressed fingers on potato and followed a picnic table to a bowl of chutney. Now we ask what these tiny beings tell us about harm, friendship and ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: The same kind of microbe can live quietly in your gut and make you ill in your food. Whether a microbe harms us depends on where she is, how many there are, and who meets her. So 'harmful' describes a meeting, not a kind of microbe.
deep_truth.habit: We sort germs into good germs and bad germs, as if each microbe carried the label inside her. We also sort people into clean people and unclean people, though a healthy cook can carry typhoid.
deep_truth.evidence: In the yeast test, the same yeast was useful in idli batter and a nuisance in a sugary drink. In the potato test, the microbes on a clean-looking finger did nothing on skin and grew into colonies on moist potato. E. coli lives in almost every gut, and only a few strains make people ill. If your results differ, write them as they are.

three.who_am_i: You carry about as many bacterial cells as you have cells of your own. Most of them help you digest, so you are a crowd of beings living together.
three.what_is_life: A bacterium in a pot of warm dal is not trying to harm anyone. She eats and makes more of herself, as every living being does. We call it illness when her meal and our body meet.
three.what_is_this_world: A gut, a kitchen counter and a pond are all places where trillions of tiny beings meet. Who does well there depends on food, water and warmth.

roots.thread: Your lunch is a meal for you and for a crowd of beings too small to see. In your gut, bacteria and you share the work of digesting it. In a dal left in the sun, bacteria eat without you. The beings are the same in both places. What changes is the place, the warmth, the numbers and who is eating. Keeping food safe is not a war on microbes. It is learning how to share a kitchen with them.

teachings.teaching: When food is eaten, it divides into three parts. The coarsest part leaves the body, the middle part builds the body, and the finest part builds the mind. Mind is made of food.
teachings.link: The same food that becomes you can become a million microbes. Who the food becomes depends on who reaches it first, and how warm it is.

teachings.teaching: Eat of what the earth gives that is lawful and good.
teachings.link: The word translated as good means wholesome and pure. Food that is good is not only tasty, but safe to eat.

teachings.teaching: A person needs no medicine if they eat only after the last meal has been digested.
teachings.link: Timing is part of health. In this unit we learned that timing matters for food too, since cooked food that waits many hours in the warmth becomes a home for microbes.

science.text: Most of the bacteria in the human gut are harmless or helpful, and the body holds roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells.
How much the mix of gut microbes affects mood, weight and long-term illness is being studied, and many claims are not yet proven.

other_view.view: However we think about microbes, the kitchen rules stay simple and strict. Keep microbes out of food that will not be cooked. Keep food out of the danger zone. Wash hands. Thinking that microbes are only doing what living beings do must never make us careless, since people have died of food poisoning.

practice.title: Twenty seconds of soap
practice.say: Wet your hands and put on soap. Breathe in slowly for four counts while you rub the palms. Breathe out for four counts while you rub the backs of the hands. Rub between the fingers, around the thumbs and under the nails, breathing slowly the whole time. Keep going for twenty seconds. Rinse, dry well, and notice how your hands feel.
practice.kid: Wet your hands. Add soap. Rub slowly for twenty seconds. Breathe in and out. Rinse. Dry well.

ask: If most of the microbes in and on you are harmless, why do we wash our hands at all?
Is a bacterium in your dal an enemy, or just someone who found a meal?
Where does the 'you' end and the microbes begin?

printables.title: Tally table: one row for each food, with four columns
items: Column 1: ate this food and became ill.
Column 2: ate this food and stayed well.
Column 3: did not eat this food and became ill.
Column 4: did not eat this food and stayed well.
One row for each of the four foods, and one empty row for a food you want to add.

rules: Read the mystery aloud. Mystery A is a birthday party in Hyderabad with 16 guests and 4 foods: samosa, paneer roll, mango lassi and fruit chaat. Some guests were ill the next day.
Lay out the guest cards. Draw the tally table, with one row for each food and four columns.

Take the guest cards one at a time. For each food, make a mark in the right column of that food's row. A guest who ate the samosa and was ill goes in column 1 of the samosa row. A guest who did not eat the samosa and was ill goes in column 3 of the samosa row.
When all the cards are done, add up each column.
For each food, work out two fractions. First, of those who ate it, how many were ill? Then, of those who did not eat it, how many were ill?
The suspect is the food where the first fraction is much bigger than the second. A food that everyone ate cannot be the suspect, because it cannot tell the ill guests from the well ones.
Say how sure you are. A table points to a suspect, but it does not prove it. Say one thing you would test in the laboratory, or one question you would ask the cook.

Scoring: 3 points for naming the right suspect, 2 points for the right fractions and 1 point for saying what you would test. The player with the most points wins. If you play alone, try to score all 6 on both mysteries.

Paneer roll, 9 ate and 5 ill, 7 did not eat and 4 ill. Mango lassi, 7 ate and 4 ill, 9 did not eat and 5 ill. Fruit chaat, 10 ate and 8 ill, 6 did not eat and 1 ill.

flow.context: In this step you work out the fractions for each food and name the suspect.
flow.do: For each food, write two fractions. The first is the ill ones among those who ate it. The second is the ill ones among those who did not. Circle the food with the biggest gap. Name your suspect.
flow.say: For each food, how many of those who ate it were ill? How many of those who did not eat it were ill? Which food has the biggest difference?
flow.kid: Work out two fractions for each food. Circle the biggest gap. Name the suspect.

check.q: For one food, 8 of the 10 guests who ate it were ill, and 1 of the 6 who did not eat it was ill. What does this tell you?
options: The food is a strong suspect, as most eaters were ill and few non-eaters were
The food is safe, because someone who did not eat it was ill
The food cannot be told apart from the others

games.title: Bio, Chemical or Stone? Sorting kitchen hazards
games.context: This is a sorting game with 20 kitchen cards. For each card you decide whether the hazard is a microbe, a chemical or a hard object, and what to do about it. You find out that the three kinds need different fixes.

setup.caption: 1. Make four labelled spaces on a table: biological, chemical, physical and safe.

setup.caption: 2. Shuffle the 20 cards. The reader takes the top card and reads the front.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards: a kitchen situation on the front, and the answer with the fix on the back

items.f: Small stones in a plate of rice.
items.b: PHYSICAL. A hard object that can break a tooth. Pick and wash the rice before cooking.

items.f: Cooked rice left in a pot on the counter all night in May.
items.b: BIOLOGICAL. Tough spores in rice wake up and grow in the warmth and make a toxin. Cool rice quickly and put it in the fridge within two hours.

items.f: Groundnuts with grey-green dust on them.
items.b: CHEMICAL. A mould has made a toxin called aflatoxin, and cooking does not remove it. Throw them away.

items.f: Pesticide spray still on the skin of an unwashed brinjal.
items.b: CHEMICAL. A poison put on the crop to kill pests. Rinse under running water and rub, or peel.

items.f: A tiny piece of broken glass in a jar of jam.
items.b: PHYSICAL. Glass can cut the mouth and gut. Do not eat it, and tell the shop.

items.f: A cook with loose motions and vomiting making food for a feast.
items.b: BIOLOGICAL. Her gut microbes can reach the food through her hands. She should stay out of the kitchen until she has been well for a day or two.

items.f: Floor-cleaning liquid kept in an old cold-drink bottle on a kitchen shelf.
items.b: CHEMICAL. A child could drink it, thinking it is a drink. Keep cleaners in their own labelled bottles, away from food.

items.f: A long hair in the dal.
items.b: PHYSICAL. It is rarely harmful, but it shows the cook's hair was not tied back or covered. Tie back or cover the hair.

items.f: A cook with an uncovered cut on her finger mixing a salad.
items.b: BIOLOGICAL. Staphylococcus lives in cuts and on skin, and can make a toxin in food. Cover cuts with a waterproof plaster and wear a glove.

items.f: A knife used on raw fish and then on cucumber, without washing.
items.b: BIOLOGICAL. Microbes from the raw fish move onto the cucumber, which is not cooked afterwards. Use a different knife and board, or wash with soap and hot water in between.

items.f: A jar of lemon pickle, closed, taken from with a dry spoon.
items.b: SAFE. Salt, acid and oil leave microbes little water to use, and the dry spoon adds none.

items.f: A packet of milk puffed up like a balloon.
items.b: BIOLOGICAL. Microbes inside are making gas. Do not open it or drink it. Throw it away.

items.f: Bright colour in sweets that is not an approved food colour.
items.b: CHEMICAL. A cheap colour that is not meant for food can be harmful. Buy from shops you trust, and look for the licence number.

items.f: A small bone in a fish curry served to a toddler.
items.b: PHYSICAL. A bone can choke a child. Remove bones before serving.

items.f: Red kidney beans (rajma) cooked for only a few minutes.
items.b: CHEMICAL. Raw rajma holds a natural poison that makes people sick. Soak, then boil hard for at least ten minutes.

items.f: A potato with green patches and sprouts.
items.b: CHEMICAL. The green parts hold a natural poison called solanine. Cut away the green parts and the sprouts, or throw the potato away.

items.f: Salad washed with water from a tank that has not been cleaned for years.
items.b: BIOLOGICAL. Dirty water carries microbes that can cause illness. Use safe water, boiled or filtered, to wash food that is eaten raw.

items.f: Fresh coriander washed under running water until the water runs clear.
items.b: SAFE. Running water moves soil and microbes away from the leaves.

items.f: A fly walking over a plate of cut fruit left uncovered.
items.b: BIOLOGICAL. Flies carry microbes on their feet and mouths. Cover food with a lid, a plate or a net.

items.f: Tiny wire bristles from a steel scrubber in a steel dabba.
items.b: PHYSICAL. Bristles can break off and stay in a dabba, and then in the food. Check dabbas after scrubbing, and replace worn scrubbers.

printables.title: Answer slips: biological, chemical, physical and safe
items: Biological: microbes such as bacteria, mould and viruses.
Chemical: poisons, whether made by people or by nature.
Physical: hard or sharp objects such as stones, glass and bones.
Safe: no hazard here. The food is handled well.

rules: Shuffle the 20 cards. One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud, without showing the back.
Everyone else puts a slip in the space they choose: biological, chemical, physical or safe. Then everyone turns their slip over together.
Each player says one thing a cook could do to fix the problem. The fix does not need to match the card. It only needs to make sense.
The reader reads the back. A player who chose the right kind scores 2 points. A player with a sensible fix scores 1 more point.
Pass the pile to the next reader after each card. The reader does not score on their own card.
Play until every card is read. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: read the front, choose a slip, say your fix aloud, then turn the card over. Score yourself, and try to beat 30 points out of 60.

flow.say: Biological means a living thing, such as bacteria or mould. Chemical means a poison. Physical means a hard or sharp object. Safe means there is nothing to worry about.
flow.kid: Make four spaces. Read the meanings. Shuffle the cards.
flow.parent: Read the answer slips aloud. Note that natural poisons, such as aflatoxin, count as chemical hazards, although a mould made them.

flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a space. Say a fix.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Bio, Chemical or Stone game. You talk about which kind of hazard needs the most care.

flow.say: Which kind of hazard can you see, and which kind can you not see? Which kind would you check first in your own kitchen?
flow.kid: Which hazards can you see? Which can you not see?
flow.think: Which cards showed hazards that you could fix just by looking?
flow.parent: Microbes and natural toxins cannot be seen, so they need habits such as washing, cooling and separating. Stones and glass can be seen, so they need care and attention.

experiments.title: Yeast in Four Places: how does temperature change how fast microbes grow?
experiments.context: In this experiment, you divide a sugary yeast mixture between four glasses. You put them in a fridge, on a counter, in a warm-water bath, and one after heating it. Foam shows how fast the yeast grows.
experiments.question: How do cold, room temperature, warmth and heat change how fast yeast grows in sugary water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess which glass will have the most foam after two hours, and which will have the least. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All four glasses start with the same mixture, the same amount and the same glass. They stand on the same kind of surface, and you measure them at the same times. Only the temperature is different, so any difference in foam comes from the temperature.
results_table: D: heated first, then counter (centimetres of foam)

materials.item: 4 clear glasses or jars of the same size, tall rather than wide, each holding about 250 millilitres
1 packet of dry baking yeast (about 7 grams), the kind sold for bread
4 level teaspoons of sugar
800 millilitres of lukewarm water, comfortable on the inside of your wrist
a jug, a teaspoon and a small steel pan
a bowl big enough to hold one glass, and a jug of hand-hot water (hot, but comfortable to hold your finger in for 10 seconds)
4 rubber bands or strips of tape, a marker, a ruler and a clock
a tray to stand the glasses on, and a fridge

experiments.safety: A grown-up heats the pan for glass D and handles all hot water. Steam can scald, so keep children away from the stove. Never taste the yeast mixture. Do not seal the glasses with a lid, because the gas can build up. Wash your hands afterwards, and a grown-up pours the mixture down the sink.
experiments.record: Fill in the table every 30 minutes for two hours. At the end, draw the four glasses side by side with their foam, and write what you think, what you saw and why.

setup.art: A jug with lukewarm water, sugar and yeast being stirred, with foam starting to form.
setup.caption: 1. Stir sugar and yeast into lukewarm water in a jug.

setup.art: Four glasses with 200 millilitres of the mixture in each, and a rubber band marking the top of the liquid in each glass.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the same amount into four glasses and mark the level with a rubber band.

setup.art: A grown-up heating the mixture for one glass in a small pan until it steams, then pouring it back into glass D.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up heats the mixture for glass D until it steams, then lets it cool.

setup.art: Four glasses in four places: one in a fridge, one on a counter, one standing in a bowl of warm water, and one on the counter beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Put A in the fridge, B on the counter, C in a warm-water bath and D on the counter.

setup.art: A child measuring the foam on a glass against a ruler held beside the rubber band.
setup.caption: 5. Every 30 minutes, measure the foam above the rubber band.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Yeast in Four Places test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the four glasses and the places they will go. Say that one glass will be heated first. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: The same yeast and the same sugar will go into four glasses. One goes in the fridge. One stays on the counter. One goes in a warm-water bath. One is heated first. Which will foam the most? Which the least? Why?
flow.kid: Four glasses of yeast. Fridge, counter, warm bath, heated. Which foams most? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that glass will foam the most?
good: Warmth helps yeast to grow.
Yeast likes warm places.
The fridge will slow it down.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Yeast is a microbe that eats sugar and makes the gas that makes the foam. More foam means more yeast, busy and growing.

flow.context: In this step, you make the yeast mixture and fill the four glasses. A grown-up heats the mixture for glass D.
flow.do: In the jug, stir 4 level teaspoons of sugar and the whole packet of yeast into 800 millilitres of lukewarm water. Wait 5 minutes. Pour 200 millilitres into each of glasses A, B and C. Pour 200 millilitres into a small pan, and a grown-up heats it until it steams. Keep it hot for 2 minutes. Pour it into glass D and let it cool for 15 minutes.
flow.say: This mixture is full of yeast. Glasses A, B and C get it just as it is. Glass D is heated until it steams, so the heat will show what it does to the yeast. Never taste any of it.
flow.kid: Stir sugar and yeast into warm water. Pour 200 millilitres into each glass. A grown-up heats D.

check.q: Why do we heat the mixture for glass D until it steams?
options: To find out what heat does to yeast
To make the mixture sweeter
To make glass D prettier
check.why: Glass D shows what happens when microbes are heated a lot. If D stays flat while the others foam, we know that heat can stop yeast growing. This is the same reason that cooking makes food safer.

flow.parent: The water for the mixture should be lukewarm, like a bath for a baby. If it is too hot, it will kill the yeast in all the glasses and nothing will happen. Use a tray, because foam can spill.

flow.context: In this step, you put each glass in its place and mark the starting level.
flow.do: Put a rubber band around each glass at the top of the liquid. Put A on a shelf in the fridge. Put B on the counter, in the shade. Stand C in a bowl of hand-hot water. Put D on the counter next to B, once it is lukewarm. Write down the time.
flow.say: Mark the top of the liquid with a rubber band. A goes in the fridge. B goes on the counter. C stands in a bowl of hand-hot water. D sits beside B. Write down the time, so we know when to measure.
flow.kid: Mark the liquid level. A to the fridge. B on the counter. C in warm water. D beside B.
flow.parent: Change the water in C's bowl for fresh hand-hot water after an hour, since it cools. Check that D is lukewarm before it goes on the counter, so it starts like the others. Write the room temperature if you can.

flow.context: In this step, you measure the foam on each glass every 30 minutes, four times, and write the results in the table.
flow.do: At 30, 60, 90 and 120 minutes, measure the foam above the rubber band on each glass with the ruler. Take glass A out of the fridge for the measurement, then put it back. Write the measurements in the table.
flow.say: Look at the foam on each glass and measure it from the rubber band. Which glass has the most? Which has none? Is the order changing?
flow.kid: Every 30 minutes, measure the foam. Write it in the table.
flow.wait: Wait 30 minutes between measurements. Four measurements take two hours.
flow.parent: Typical: glass C foams well within 30 to 60 minutes, often several centimetres. Glass B foams more slowly, and faster in a hot kitchen. Glass A hardly changes. Glass D should stay flat. If D foams, the heating was not enough, and the test should be repeated. Write down what really happens.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Yeast in Four Places test. You compare the glasses and say what you found.
flow.do: Put the glasses side by side. Compare the foam. Check your guess from step 1. Say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Which glass foamed most? Which least? Was your guess right? Tell me what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.kid: Look at the four glasses. Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

check.q: Glass A, in the fridge, has hardly any foam. Does that mean the yeast in it is dead?
options: No, the cold slowed her growth and she is still alive
Yes, the cold killed her
Yes, the fridge took her sugar away
check.why: Cold slows microbes a great deal, but does not kill them. If you took glass A out and warmed it, the yeast would start to foam. This is why a fridge slows food spoilage, but does not stop it.

flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: warmth makes yeast grow faster, cold slows her, and heat stops her. What I saw: glass C had the most foam, A had almost none, and D stayed flat. Why: yeast is a living being, and her growth speeds up with warmth until it gets too hot. Link to the card: The danger zone.

experiments.title: Handprints on a Potato: does washing really matter?
experiments.context: In this experiment, you press unwashed, rinsed and soap-washed fingers onto cooked potato slices that are sealed in bags. You see how many microbes grow from each. You never open the bags.
experiments.question: Do fingers carry fewer microbes after a quick rinse with water, or after washing with soap for 20 seconds?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess which potato slice will grow the most spots, and which will grow the fewest. Will a quick rinse be enough? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The slices come from one potato, cooked together and cut with the same clean knife. The same finger is used each time, pressed for the same 5 seconds, after being dirtied in the same way. All the bags sit side by side on one shelf. Only what was done to the finger is different.

materials.item: 1 medium potato
4 clear zip-lock bags, sandwich size, brand new
a saucepan with a lid, and a clean knife
a pair of clean tongs or two clean forks
tape, a marker and a sheet of paper
an old shoe, soap, running water and a clean cloth
a shelf at room temperature, out of the sun

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the potato and cuts it. Never open the bags once they are sealed, and never smell them, because some of the growth may be harmful. Keep little children away from the bags. At the end, a grown-up puts the closed bags into a rubbish bag, ties it, and puts it in the outside bin. Wash your hands after rubbing your finger on the shoe, and after touching the bags.

schedule.what: Guess. A grown-up boils and cuts the potato. Press each finger on its slice. Seal and tape the bags.
Look at the bags without opening them. Count the spots. Write them down.
Look again. Count the spots. Write them down.
Look and count. Compare. Draw the four slices. Say what you think, what you saw and why. A grown-up disposes of the bags.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. On day 7, draw the four bags side by side and shade the spots and fuzzy patches you can see. Write what you think, what you saw and why.

setup.art: A whole potato boiling in a pan, with a lid, and a grown-up beside the stove.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up boils the potato until it is soft.

setup.art: A clean knife cutting the cooked potato into four slices on a clean plate, with tongs lifting a slice into a zip-lock bag.
setup.caption: 2. Cut four slices. Put each in a clean bag with the tongs.

setup.art: A child rubbing a finger on a shoe sole, then pressing the finger on a potato slice inside an open bag.
setup.caption: 3. Dirty a finger. Press it on slice B for 5 seconds.

setup.art: A child washing a finger with soap for 20 seconds at a tap, and a timer showing 20.
setup.caption: 4. Wash a finger with soap for 20 seconds. Press it on slice D.

setup.art: Four sealed bags in a row on a shelf, labelled A, B, C and D, each with a different number of spots.
setup.caption: 5. Seal and tape the bags. Look at them every two days without opening.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Handprints on a Potato test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Explain the four slices. A is not touched. B is touched with a dirty finger. C is touched after a quick rinse with water. D is touched after soap and 20 seconds of washing. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: We will press a finger on each of four potato slices. Slice A is not touched. B gets a dirty finger. C gets a finger rinsed with water. D gets a finger washed with soap. Which will grow the most? Which the least? Why?
flow.kid: Four slices. Which grows most? Which grows least? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Do you think a quick rinse is as good as soap? Why?
good: Water alone should wash it off.
Soap is needed to take the oil off.
I'm not sure.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.

flow.context: In this step, a grown-up boils the potato and cuts four slices. Boiling makes the slices almost free of microbes at the start.
flow.do: Boil the potato for 15 minutes. Wash the knife and a plate in very hot water. Cut four slices, each about 1 centimetre thick. Use clean tongs to put each slice into its own bag. Do not touch the slices. Label the bags A, B, C and D, and leave them open.
flow.say: Boiling kills most of the microbes in the potato. So the slices start clean. If anything grows, it must have come from the air, or from the finger. We use tongs, so our hands do not touch the slices.
flow.kid: A grown-up boils the potato. Slice it with a clean knife. Use tongs. Do not touch.
flow.parent: Let the slices cool for a few minutes before you put them in the bags. Do not wipe the slices or the knife with a cloth. Wash the knife and plate in very hot water and let them air dry. Write A to D on the bags with the marker.

flow.context: In this step, you press the fingers on the slices and seal the bags. Each finger is cleaned in a different way.
flow.do: Slice A: open and close the bag without touching the slice. Slice B: rub your finger on the sole of a shoe for 10 seconds. Press it on slice B for 5 seconds. Slice C: rub your finger on the shoe again. Rinse it under the tap for 5 seconds and dry it on a clean cloth. Press it on slice C. Slice D: rub your finger on the shoe again. Wash it with soap for 20 seconds, rinse and dry it. Press it on slice D. Seal each bag and put tape across the seal.
flow.say: We use the same finger every time. First it gets dirty again, and then it is cleaned in a different way. B is not cleaned at all. C is a quick rinse. D is soap for twenty seconds. Press for five seconds each. Then seal and tape the bag.
flow.kid: Dirty your finger. Clean it in a different way for each slice. Press for 5 seconds. Seal.

check.q: Slice A is not touched by a finger, but its bag is opened and closed. Why do we do that?
options: To see how much grows from the air alone
To make the slice colder
To give the slice a rest
check.why: Slice A shows how much grows on a clean slice in the same bag. If A also has spots, we know some microbes came from the air or the bag, and we can tell what the fingers added.

flow.parent: Use the same finger of the same hand each time. A child's dry fingers pick up less than a damp or sticky finger, so rub the finger on the shoe each time for the same time. Wash your own hands after this step.

flow.context: In this step, you look at the sealed bags on days 3, 5 and 7, and count the spots and fuzzy patches.
flow.do: Look at each bag without opening it. Count the round spots and the fuzzy patches. Write the numbers in the table. If there are too many to count, write many.
flow.say: Look through the bag without opening it. Do you see round spots? Do you see fuzzy patches? Count them. Which bag has the most today?
flow.kid: Look at each bag. Do not open it. Count the spots. Write them down.
flow.wait: Look at the bags on days 3, 5 and 7.
flow.parent: Spots are colonies of bacteria or yeast, each grown from one microbe or a few. Fuzzy patches are moulds. The first spots usually show on day 2 or 3. Never open a bag, and never smell it. If a bag is leaking, put it in a second bag and a grown-up puts it in the outside bin.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Handprints on a Potato test. You compare the four bags and say what you found. A grown-up then disposes of the bags.
flow.do: Put the four bags side by side. Compare the spots and patches. Check your guess from step 1. Draw the four slices. Say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why. A grown-up puts the closed bags in the outside bin.
flow.say: Which slice grew most? Which least? Did soap make a difference? Tell me what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.kid: Compare the four bags. Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

check.q: Slice D, from the finger washed with soap, had fewer spots than slice B, from the dirty finger, but still had some. What does this show?
options: Soap and rubbing take off many microbes but not all
Soap kills every microbe
Soap makes no difference
check.why: Washing lowers the number of microbes a great deal, but a washed hand is not sterile. That is why we also wash again after touching raw meat, and why a clean-looking hand can still carry some microbes.

flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: soap and 20 seconds of washing take most microbes off the finger, and a quick rinse takes fewer. What I saw: slice B had the most spots, and D had fewer than C. Why: soap lifts oily dirt and microbes, and the water carries them away. If your result differs, such as C having fewer than D, write it down. One finger and one potato is a small test. Link to the card: How soap works.

experiments.title: Salt Pulls Water Out: what a pickle does to a cucumber slice
experiments.context: In this experiment, you sprinkle salt on some cucumber slices, sugar on others, and nothing on the rest. You find out which pulls out the most water, as a pickle does to a microbe.
experiments.question: Which pulls more water out of a cucumber slice in an hour: a teaspoon of salt, a teaspoon of sugar, or nothing?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess which plate will have the most liquid after an hour, and which the least. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the slices come from one cucumber, cut to the same thickness. Each plate holds four slices in one layer and sits tilted the same way. You use one level teaspoon of salt or sugar. Only the sprinkle is different, so any difference comes from the sprinkle.
results_table: How a slice feels when you bend it

materials.item: 1 firm cucumber, washed
3 flat plates with a rim, all the same
1 level teaspoon of salt
1 level teaspoon of fine sugar
a teaspoon for measuring, and a clean knife
a folded cloth or a small book to tilt each plate
a clock, a marker and sticky labels
a ruler to check the thickness of the slices

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the cucumber with the knife. The cucumber slices are safe to eat afterwards, since they have only had salt or sugar on clean plates, but do not eat slices that have been sitting for more than a few hours.
experiments.record: Fill in the table at 30 minutes and 60 minutes. Draw one slice from each plate, with the liquid around it. Write what you think, what you saw and why.

setup.art: A cucumber being cut into thin even slices of 5 millimetres on a board, with a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts 12 slices, each 5 millimetres thick.

setup.art: Three plates each with four cucumber slices laid in one layer, labelled plain, salt and sugar.
setup.caption: 2. Put 4 slices on each of three plates. Label them plain, salt and sugar.

setup.art: A level teaspoon of salt being sprinkled over the slices on one plate, with another plate having sugar.
setup.caption: 3. Sprinkle a level teaspoon of salt on one plate, and sugar on the next.

setup.art: The three plates tilted on a folded cloth with a clock showing the time, and a puddle gathering at the low edge.
setup.caption: 4. Tilt each plate a little. Wait 30 minutes and look.

setup.art: A child spooning the liquid from the low edge of a plate into a teaspoon and counting.
setup.caption: 5. Spoon up the liquid and count the teaspoons. Bend a slice from each plate.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Salt Pulls Water Out test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the cucumber, the salt and the sugar. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: We will sprinkle salt on some cucumber slices and sugar on others, and leave some plain. After an hour, which plate will have the most liquid? Why?
flow.kid: Salt, sugar or nothing on cucumber. Which gets the most liquid? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that plate will have the most liquid?
good: Salt takes water out.
The cucumber has lots of water inside.
Sugar will melt and make a puddle.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.

flow.context: In this step, a grown-up cuts the cucumber into twelve slices of the same thickness.
flow.do: Wash the cucumber. A grown-up cuts 12 slices, each about 5 millimetres thick. Check a few against the ruler. Put 4 slices in one layer on each plate.
flow.say: All the slices must be the same thickness, so that the plates are fair. A thicker slice would hold more water. Put four on each plate in a single layer.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts 12 slices. Check them with the ruler. Put 4 on each plate.

check.q: Why must all the cucumber slices be the same thickness?
options: So that only the sprinkle is different
So that they look tidy
So that the plates are heavier
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one plate had thicker slices, it might give more liquid just because it held more water, and we would not know if the salt was the reason.

flow.context: In this step, you sprinkle the salt and the sugar, and tilt the plates so the liquid runs to one edge.
flow.do: Label the plates plain, salt and sugar. Sprinkle a level teaspoon of salt over the slices on the salt plate. Sprinkle a level teaspoon of sugar over the sugar plate. Put nothing on the plain plate. Tilt each plate a little with a folded cloth. Write the time.
flow.say: Salt on one plate, sugar on another, nothing on the third. Tilt them a little so that any liquid runs to one corner. Write down the time. We look again in thirty minutes.
flow.kid: Salt on one. Sugar on one. Nothing on one. Tilt the plates. Write the time.
flow.parent: Tilt all three plates the same amount, on the same side. Spread the salt and sugar evenly over the slices, so that every slice gets some.

flow.context: In this step, you measure the liquid at 30 minutes and 60 minutes, and bend a slice from each plate.
flow.do: At 30 minutes, spoon up the liquid at the low edge of each plate with the teaspoon. Count the teaspoons, or write a few drops or half a teaspoon. Do the same at 60 minutes. Lift one slice from each plate, and bend it gently. Write down whether it bends easily or snaps.
flow.say: How much liquid is at the low edge of each plate? Count the teaspoons. Now bend a slice. Is it stiff, or floppy? Which plate has the floppiest slices?
flow.kid: Spoon up the liquid. Count the teaspoons. Bend a slice. Stiff or floppy?
flow.wait: Wait 30 minutes, then another 30 minutes, between looks.
flow.parent: Typical: the salt plate has one or two teaspoons by 60 minutes, and its slices are limp. The sugar plate has less, and the plain plate has a few drops, with stiff slices. Exact numbers differ. Salt is sprinkled as grains, which may draw water faster than the sugar grains.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Salt Pulls Water Out test. You say what you found, and connect it to pickles and microbes.
flow.do: Compare the three plates. Check your guess from step 1. Say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Which plate had the most liquid? Which slices felt floppiest? Where did that water come from? Tell me what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.kid: Compare the plates. Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

check.q: A microbe is a tiny cell with a thin skin that lets water through. What happens to her in a very salty pickle?
options: Water leaves her, and she shrivels and cannot grow
She drinks the salty water and grows bigger
Nothing happens to her
check.why: Water moves through the thin skin towards the saltier side. In a salty pickle, water leaves the microbe, as it left the cucumber slices, and she shrivels. This is how salt, and sugar in jam, keep food safe.

flow.think: If salt and sugar keep food safe, why can a pickle still grow mould if you put a wet spoon in it?
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: salt pulls out the most water, sugar a little, and plain slices keep theirs. What I saw: the salt plate had a puddle and floppy slices. Why: water moves through the cucumber's thin skin towards the saltier side. Link to the card: How salt, sugar and drying keep food safe.

activities.title: Read the Packet: five labels, five questions
activities.context: In this activity, you collect five food packets from the kitchen and read each label like a detective. You find out what the dates, marks and numbers on the packet are for.

materials.item: 5 different packets or jars of food from the kitchen, such as biscuits, namkeen, noodles, jam, and packet milk or paneer
a sheet of paper and a pencil, ruled into columns
a magnifying glass, if you have one (optional)
a calculator, if you have one (optional)

schedule.what: Guess what the first ingredient is. Read six things on each label. Compare them. Decide what should go in the fridge.

activities.record: A table with a row for each packet and columns for: the first three ingredients, the type of date, the vegetarian mark, the licence number, the allergens and the storage advice.

setup.art: Five food packets of different kinds laid out in a row on a kitchen table, with a notebook and pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out five packets and make a table.
